articles.title: How to Build an Integrated Project Baseline You Can Trust
articles.excerpt: Connect scope, schedule, cost and change in one usable control framework, with a worked example and a practical checklist for your next baseline review.
articles.image_alt: Project professionals collaborating in a modern workplace
articles.content:
A project can have a detailed programme, an approved budget and a risk register while still lacking a usable basis for control. The documents may describe different versions of the work. A variance report can then be mathematically correct and operationally misleading.

An integrated baseline gives the team a consistent reference for explaining what was authorised, what has changed and what the latest evidence suggests. This guide offers a practical way to build that reference without turning every reporting cycle into a reconciliation exercise.

## Start with the decision your baseline must support

Ask the sponsor what they need to decide during delivery. Typical questions include whether a milestone remains achievable, whether a proposed change is affordable, and which intervention deserves management attention. Work backwards from those questions to the information the team must maintain.

APM describes project controls as connecting scope, time, cost, risk and change with performance analysis and forecasting. That is the professional context for this guide; the review questions and fictional example below are an editorial application of those principles. See [APM's introduction to project controls](https://www.apm.org.uk/resources/what-is-project-management/what-is-project-controls/).

## 1. Define a work package everyone recognises

Choose a manageable unit of work with a named owner, a clear output and an acceptance condition. Give it a stable identifier that appears in the schedule, estimate, purchasing records and reporting structure.

For example, WP-140 might mean an accepted equipment installation, including inspection and handover records. If the cost team uses WP-140 only for purchasing while the planner uses it for purchasing and installation, their numbers will not describe the same accomplishment. Resolve that difference before approval.

Record exclusions as carefully as inclusions. A package can appear comfortably within budget simply because testing or disposal has been left outside the estimate.

## 2. Connect time and money to the same work

For each package, identify the activities, dependencies, accountable resources and budget basis. Agree how costs will be assigned to reporting periods and how progress will be evidenced. Keep the reporting cut-off consistent so that a Friday schedule update is not compared with costs posted only to the preceding Tuesday.

| Baseline element | Question for the package owner |
| --- | --- |
| Scope | What output must be accepted, and by whom? |
| Schedule | What must happen first, and what follows? |
| Budget | Which quantities, rates and assumptions support the allowance? |
| Progress | What objective evidence demonstrates completion? |
| Risk | Which uncertainties could change the forecast? |
| Approval | Who can authorise a change to the commitment? |

Keep the source and version beside each answer. Another colleague should be able to reconstruct the basis of the commitment without relying on the original estimator's memory.

## 3. Keep the baseline and current forecast distinct

Consider a fictional package with an approved budget of £120,000 and a six-week delivery window. A supplier advises that a component will arrive ten working days late. The latest forecast may therefore show a later finish and additional supervision costs.

Retain the authorised reference, update the forecast and explain the movement. Present recovery options with their consequences: resequencing might protect another activity, while expediting might have a cost and require approval. Neither option is automatically the right answer.

A forecast is the current assessment of the likely outcome. A baseline is the authorised reference against which movement is explained. Keeping both visible helps the sponsor distinguish changed circumstances from unapproved scope growth or weak original assumptions.

## 4. Make changes traceable

A usable change record connects a request to its scope, time, cost, risk and benefits implications, the decision maker and the approval date. APM's [change control guidance](https://www.apm.org.uk/resources/what-is-project-management/what-is-change-control/) explains the evaluation and approval of proposed baseline changes.

After approval, update the connected records together. If a scope change increases the budget but its associated activities never enter the schedule, the baseline becomes inconsistent again. Preserve the previous version and a concise explanation of the authorised movement.

## 5. Reconcile before reporting

Ask a package owner to walk through one item from accepted scope to progress evidence, posted cost and forecast completion. This is often more revealing than another slide of aggregate percentages.

- Check that package identifiers match across current reporting files.
- Confirm costs, commitments and accrual assumptions do not double-count the same obligation.
- Separate approved changes from proposals awaiting a decision.
- Explain the largest forecast movements and identify their owners.
- Record unresolved data gaps and the dates they will be corrected.

## Put it into practice

Select one active package and create a one-page baseline record using the questions above. Ask its planner, cost owner and delivery lead to review it together. Document disagreements and agree who will resolve them before using the package in a management recommendation.

Continue with our [schedule health review](/articles/schedule-health-checks-before-trusting-a-finish-date) and [earned value example](/articles/earned-value-management-worked-example) to examine the time and cost implications.

## Professional reading

- [APM: What is project controls?](https://www.apm.org.uk/resources/what-is-project-management/what-is-project-controls/)
- [APM: What is change control?](https://www.apm.org.uk/resources/what-is-project-management/what-is-change-control/)

The package and figures are fictional learning examples, not reported client or learner outcomes.

articles.title: Seven Schedule Health Checks Before You Trust a Finish Date
articles.excerpt: Review logic, progress, resources and critical activities before presenting a delivery forecast. Includes a simple dependency example and a review meeting agenda.
articles.content:
A date at the end of a Gantt chart can look precise without being dependable. The useful question is whether the underlying model explains how the team can get there, using current evidence and resources that actually exist.

Before presenting a completion date to a sponsor, use these checks to identify where the forecast needs investigation. They are a practical discussion aid, not a substitute for full schedule assurance or your organisation's planning requirements.

## Understand what you are reviewing

The US Government Accountability Office's [Schedule Assessment Guide](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-16-89g) is a comprehensive reference for schedule quality. It addresses completeness, logical sequencing, resources, durations, traceability, critical paths, float, risk, updates and baseline maintenance.

Our seven checks turn that concern for schedule credibility into questions for a delivery conversation. They do not reproduce or replace GAO's ten best practices.

## 1. Does the plan include the work needed for acceptance?

Start at the contractual or operational finish and work backwards. Ask what evidence will allow the customer to accept the result. Missing inspection, commissioning, training or documentation can leave a plan apparently complete while the deliverable remains unusable.

Choose one handover milestone and ask its owner to list the prerequisites without looking at the schedule. Compare that list with the model. A missing dependency deserves a resolution, even if adding it makes the published date less comfortable.

## 2. Are dependencies explained by the work?

Review activities without predecessors or successors, except where a genuine start or finish justifies that position. Ask whether each connection represents a real dependency rather than an attempt to align the chart with a desired date.

For a fictional sequence, design approval takes five working days, manufacture takes eight and inspection takes two. If sequential under one calendar, the chain requires fifteen working days. A twelve-day promise needs an explained change: overlapping work, a shorter task or an earlier start. Typing a constraint into the software is not an explanation.

## 3. Is the update supported by evidence?

Confirm one reporting cut-off. Ask for the actual start, actual finish and remaining work on a selection of active tasks. A task described as nearly complete needs a credible account of what remains, including review and rework.

If work started before its predecessor finished, investigate. The team may have found a valid overlap or started only a preparatory portion. Update the model to represent the delivery approach rather than letting software preserve an obsolete assumption.

## 4. Are people and equipment available?

Ask named resource owners about the busiest periods. A plan assigning one specialist to three simultaneous full-time tasks may be logically connected and still unachievable.

Record the resolution: different sequencing, approved capacity, reduced scope or a revised forecast. Do not treat a supplier's unconfirmed offer as committed availability. Keep uncertainty visible until its owner confirms the arrangement.

## 5. Does the driving path make operational sense?

Ask the planner to explain the chain currently driving the required finish. Then ask the delivery lead whether it reflects the work they are managing.

Review near-critical sequences too. Focusing only on one highlighted chain can overlook another with little remaining flexibility. Identify where management attention could affect the outcome, rather than simply reproducing the tool's colour scheme.

## 6. Are uncertainty and recovery options visible?

Distinguish the modelled finish from certainty. Discuss assumptions about approvals, access, productivity and supplier dates. A probability-based date should be supported by a suitable risk analysis.

For the fifteen-day fictional chain, inspection might require a scarce witness. If attendance is unconfirmed, show the dependency and the action to secure it. Do not label a date P80 merely because it feels conservative. A confidence label needs an analytical basis.

## 7. Can you explain movement since the last update?

Use a movement log instead of asking colleagues to compare large programme files. Separate actual progress, logic changes, revised durations and approved scope changes.

| Forecast movement | Evidence for the review |
| --- | --- |
| Supplier activity moved | Updated commitment and receiving impact |
| Remaining duration increased | Owner's account of unfinished work |
| Recovery activity added | Approval, resources and dependencies |
| Baseline changed | Authorised change reference and previous version |

A revised date is more useful when the decision maker can see what caused it and what remains within their influence.

## A focused review meeting

Set aside twenty minutes for one important milestone. Ask the planner to explain the driving sequence, the delivery lead to confirm remaining work, and the resource owner to confirm availability. Capture disagreements as actions with owners and dates.

Finish with one sentence: the forecast is this date, based on these assumptions, with this unresolved decision. If the team cannot complete that sentence, further assurance is needed before the forecast is presented as dependable.

Use our [integrated baseline guide](/articles/integrated-project-baseline-practical-guide) to connect movement with scope, budget and change.

## Professional reading

- [GAO: Schedule Assessment Guide](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-16-89g)

The sequence and durations are fictional learning examples. Review depth should reflect project complexity, delivery method and organisational requirements.

articles.title: Earned Value Management: A Worked Example for Project Decisions
articles.excerpt: A practical project controls guide to PV, EV, AC, CPI, SPI and cost forecasting, with a worked example and clear limits on what performance measures can tell you.
articles.content:
Spending less than planned does not necessarily mean a project is performing well. The team may simply have completed less work. Earned value management helps examine planned work, demonstrated progress and actual expenditure together.

This original fictional example explains the arithmetic and the questions that should follow. The method supports professional judgement; it does not replace review of scope, quality, schedule logic or unfinished work.

## Start with three comparable measures

Use one scope, reporting cut-off and budget basis. Planned value, or PV, is the budgeted value of work scheduled by the cut-off. Earned value, or EV, is the budgeted value of work actually accomplished. Actual cost, or AC, is the cost incurred for that accomplished work.

The [GAO Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-20-195g) provides a professional reference for cost management and EVM. The package, figures and management discussion below are an editorial teaching example, not a case study from that guide.

## The fictional package

Assume a budget at completion, or BAC, of £100,000. Ten deliverables each have an agreed budget value of £10,000. In this simplified example, a deliverable earns its value only when accepted.

At the cut-off, six deliverables were scheduled for acceptance. Four have been accepted. Cost incurred is £50,000, including an agreed accrual for work incurred but not yet invoiced.

| Measure | Calculation | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BAC | 10 deliverables × £10,000 | £100,000 |
| PV | 6 planned acceptances × £10,000 | £60,000 |
| EV | 4 actual acceptances × £10,000 | £40,000 |
| AC | Cost incurred to the cut-off | £50,000 |

Equal values are an example assumption. Real packages may need different weights and progress rules. Agree those rules before reporting; do not award value solely because time or money has been spent.

## Calculate performance

Cost variance is EV minus AC: £40,000 − £50,000 = −£10,000. Accomplished work has cost more than its budgeted value. Schedule variance is EV minus PV: £40,000 − £60,000 = −£20,000. Less budgeted work has been accomplished than planned.

CPI, the cost performance index, is EV divided by AC: £40,000 ÷ £50,000 = 0.80. SPI, the schedule performance index, is EV divided by PV: £40,000 ÷ £60,000 ≈ 0.67. Values below one signal adverse comparisons under these definitions.

The package has spent £10,000 less than the time-phased plan, but that is not a £10,000 saving. Two planned acceptances are missing. Comparing expenditure only with planned spend would hide the delivery question.

If AC or PV is zero, the corresponding index is undefined. Explain the reporting condition instead of dividing by zero or displaying a misleading performance rating.

## Forecast with explicit assumptions

A simple estimate at completion assumes observed cost efficiency continues: EAC = BAC ÷ CPI. That produces £100,000 ÷ 0.80 = £125,000. Subtracting the £50,000 incurred gives a remaining estimate to complete of £75,000.

| Forecast measure | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EAC | £100,000 ÷ 0.80 | £125,000 |
| ETC | £125,000 − £50,000 | £75,000 |
| VAC | £100,000 − £125,000 | −£25,000 |

This performance-based forecast is not a guaranteed final cost. Its credibility depends on progress measurement and whether future work will resemble completed work. A one-off mobilisation cost or a different delivery method could make the historical index a poor predictor.

Now ask the owner for an independently reasoned estimate of remaining work. If they forecast £60,000 more, their EAC is £110,000. Investigate the £15,000 difference. Which activities, rates or productivity assumptions explain the improvement? Is the necessary action approved and resourced? Preserve both calculations until the difference is understood.

## Do not turn SPI into calendar days

An SPI of 0.67 does not prove a particular number of days' delay. This calculation measures budgeted work; unfinished deliverables may sit on different schedule paths. Inspect the network, remaining durations and dependencies before making a completion-date statement.

A favourable cost index cannot establish that a deliverable meets its acceptance criteria either. If progress is credited before quality review, the apparent efficiency may disappear when rework becomes visible.

## Questions for the review

- Are EV and AC matched to the same work and cut-off?
- Is there evidence for progress rather than an unsupported percentage?
- Are invoices and accruals treated consistently?
- What caused the variance, and will it continue?
- Which forecast assumption can the owner substantiate?
- What decision is required, from whom and by when?

A useful recommendation is to review the two incomplete deliverables, confirm remaining costs and identify whether the next milestone is affected. Resolving the delivery condition matters more than changing a dashboard colour.

Review time implications with our [schedule health checks](/articles/schedule-health-checks-before-trusting-a-finish-date). For a consistent reference, start with the [baseline guide](/articles/integrated-project-baseline-practical-guide).

## Professional reading

- [GAO: Cost Estimating and Assessment Guide](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-20-195g)

All amounts and deliverables are fictional. Apply the measurement and forecasting rules agreed for your project.

articles.title: Build a Project Risk Register That Drives Action
articles.excerpt: Write clearer risk statements, distinguish risks from issues, assign response owners and connect review triggers to practical project decisions.
articles.content:
A risk register becomes useful when it changes a conversation or an action before a problem reaches the delivery team. A long list of red, amber and green entries is not enough. Each important entry should help someone understand the uncertainty, decide what to do and recognise when the response needs attention.

This guide presents an original review structure and a fictional supplier example. Use it alongside your organisation's risk process, tolerances and reporting arrangements.

## Describe the uncertainty clearly

APM's [risk management guidance](https://www.apm.org.uk/resources/what-is-project-management/what-is-risk-management/) distinguishes the cause, uncertain event and effect on objectives. It connects risk records with analysis, responses and ownership. That distinction is a useful starting point for improving an unclear entry.

The phrase supplier delay does not explain what is uncertain or which action might help. A more useful statement is: because the supplier has not yet secured a specialist component, delivery may miss the agreed dispatch window, delaying installation and increasing site support costs.

The known condition, possible event and consequences are now visible. A colleague can challenge each part: is the component unavailable, which date is threatened, and what work genuinely depends on that delivery?

## Separate risks, issues and assumptions

A risk concerns something uncertain. An issue is a condition already requiring attention. An assumption is a proposition supporting the plan that may need verification.

In the example, a possible missed dispatch is a risk. Once the supplier confirms it has missed dispatch, the event is no longer merely possible. The team needs an issue response and an updated forecast, while considering further uncertainty about recovery.

Link the risk to the issue and retain the history of the original assessment and response. It can help the team understand whether warning signs were recognised and the action was effective.

## Give the response an owner and an observable result

The risk owner is accountable for managing the risk. Individual response actions may belong to different people. Avoid assigning an action to the project team or the supplier without naming the person who will confirm completion.

| Field | Fictional supplier example |
| --- | --- |
| Risk owner | Named procurement lead |
| Immediate action | Obtain evidence of component availability |
| Action owner | Named buyer responsible for the order |
| Due point | Before the next procurement review |
| Trigger | Supplier cannot confirm the dispatch slot |
| Contingency decision | Review alternative supply or resequencing |
| Escalation | Delivery lead and authorised commercial decision maker |

These entries matter only if the named people understand and accept their responsibilities. A register records agreement; it does not create that agreement by itself.

## Make scores support a conversation

Use the probability and impact scales adopted by your organisation. State the basis for an assessment, its date and the evidence that would change the judgement. A precise-looking number without an explained scale adds little confidence.

For this supplier risk, review consequences separately: installation delay, additional support cost and the customer commitment. One combined colour could hide an important operational consequence.

Consider urgency, connections between risks, existing controls and the time available to act. A moderately rated risk needing a decision tomorrow may deserve attention before a higher-rated risk with a well-established response. Use the agreed escalation rules rather than treating a probability-impact product as the complete picture.

## Connect the register to the plan

Ask the planner where dispatch appears in the schedule and whether installation logic reflects the uncertainty. Ask the cost owner where possible support costs are considered. Ask the delivery manager which response they can implement.

Distinguish an allowance from an approved action. Budget contingency does not itself authorise a purchase or change in delivery method. Use the agreed governance route for that decision.

Apply the same discipline to opportunities. If earlier design approval could release a manufacturing slot, record the uncertainty, potential benefit and the person who can pursue it. Positive possibilities need realistic evidence too.

## End the review with action

Start with changed triggers, overdue actions and consequences affecting the next management decision. Ask owners to explain movement since the last review.

- What new evidence changes the assessment?
- Which action is complete, and what demonstrates its effectiveness?
- Which assumption remains unverified?
- Is a decision beyond the owner's authority needed?
- When will the next meaningful update be available?

For the supplier example, a useful result is a dispatch check, a named owner for an alternative sequence and a clear escalation point. Repeating the same colour for another month would not provide that result.

## A ten-minute improvement exercise

Choose three current entries. Rewrite each as a clear uncertainty statement, identify the next action and record the observation that would trigger escalation. Ask a colleague unfamiliar with the package to explain the response back to you. Clarify anything they cannot explain before the next review.

Turn the outcome into a recommendation using our [PMO reporting guide](/articles/pmo-dashboard-that-supports-decisions).

## Professional reading

- [APM: What is risk management?](https://www.apm.org.uk/resources/what-is-project-management/what-is-risk-management/)

The supplier situation is fictional. Suggested fields are an editorial working aid, not a prescribed risk standard.

articles.title: From PMO Dashboard to Decision: What Leaders Actually Need
articles.excerpt: Design reporting around the decisions leaders must make, with clear thresholds, reliable evidence, named owners and a concise decision brief.
articles.image_alt: Professional setting used to illustrate programme and portfolio governance
articles.content:
A dashboard can show dozens of indicators without making the next decision any clearer. A useful PMO report helps its audience understand what needs attention, which options are available and who has authority to act.

Start with a decision rather than a chart. Ask the sponsor which questions they expect to resolve at the next meeting. Reviewing a supplier recovery plan needs different evidence from discussing portfolio capacity or investment priorities.

## Put accountability beside the information

APM's [governance guidance](https://www.apm.org.uk/resources/what-is-project-management/what-is-governance/) connects responsibilities, delegated authority and escalation. Apply that principle to reporting: each important exception should identify the decision owner and the route for resolving it.

The layout and fictional example below are an editorial working approach, not an APM dashboard template. The right indicators and thresholds depend on the organisation and its decisions.

## Define the indicator before choosing its colour

For each measure, record its meaning, source, owner, cut-off and threshold. Explain what movement matters and what action follows. This is particularly important when combining information from projects with different reporting practices.

A budget comparison is ambiguous unless the reader knows whether it includes commitments, accruals, contingency and approved changes. A milestone measure can also mislead if one team reports contractual dates while another reports its internal working forecast.

| Reporting field | What the reader should understand |
| --- | --- |
| Definition | Exactly what is counted or compared |
| Source and cut-off | Where the figure came from and how current it is |
| Comparison | Baseline, previous forecast or approved tolerance |
| Owner | Who can explain the evidence |
| Threshold | What triggers management attention |
| Response | What action or decision is required |

Agree definitions with the people supplying the data. A visually consistent dashboard should not disguise inconsistent measurement underneath.

## Show the exception, consequence and choice

Consider a fictional package awaiting a supplier recovery proposal. Its dashboard currently shows an amber milestone. That colour alone does not tell the sponsor whether to intervene.

A better brief explains that the forecast has moved beyond an agreed tolerance, installation access is available only in a particular window, and the team needs to consider resequencing or a recovery option. Each option requires cost, schedule and uncertainty information, alongside approval requirements.

Describe the plausible alternatives, not just doing nothing and the team's preferred request. Where evidence does not support a recommendation yet, explain which check will close the gap and when it can be completed.

## Use a concise decision brief

Let the sponsor reach a supporting record without searching unrelated slides. A short brief can follow this structure:

- Decision required: the specific approval or direction requested.
- Latest useful decision point: when a choice is needed to preserve options.
- Evidence: the source, date and material limitations.
- Options: reasonable alternatives and their consequences.
- Recommendation: the proposed course and its assumptions.
- Accountability: the authorised decision maker and implementation owner.

For the supplier example, recover the programme is not a sufficiently defined decision. The request might be approval for a particular recovery activity after its scope, resources and commercial terms have been reviewed. The record should make that distinction clear.

## Report confidence and movement

Show what changed since the last review. A stable colour can hide a deteriorating forecast that has not crossed a threshold. A red indicator may remain red while a credible recovery action starts to reduce exposure.

Distinguish confirmed information from estimates and unverified assumptions. An owner's judgement can be useful, but readers need to understand its basis. If information arrives late, identify the affected period instead of silently carrying an old figure forward as current.

Review data confidence separately from delivery status. A green delivery judgement supported by incomplete information should prompt further assurance.

## Close the loop after the meeting

Record the decision, rationale, approver and conditions. Link it to the issue, change or action record. Agree how the result will appear in the next report so an approval does not disappear into meeting minutes without implementation.

At the next review, ask whether the action occurred and whether its intended effect is visible. For an approved recovery option, report actual mobilisation and the updated forecast. Raising a purchase order alone may not show that recovery is taking place.

## Improve one report this month

Choose an existing dashboard page. Move supporting detail that does not serve its audience's decision. Add clear definitions, an accountable owner and an explanation of the largest movement. Ask a reader outside the reporting team to identify the decision required.

If you want AI assistance with a narrative draft, use our [responsible AI reporting workflow](/articles/responsible-ai-project-reporting-workflow). For stronger input evidence, review the [risk register guide](/articles/project-risk-register-that-drives-action).

## Professional reading

- [APM: What is governance?](https://www.apm.org.uk/resources/what-is-project-management/what-is-governance/)

The supplier decision is fictional. Reporting and delegated authority must follow the arrangements agreed for your organisation and project.

articles.title: A Responsible AI Workflow for Project Reporting
articles.excerpt: Use AI to draft clearer reporting without surrendering control of project facts. Follow a practical workflow for approved inputs, verification and human sign-off.
articles.image_alt: Professional team collaborating on workplace information
articles.content:
AI can help turn structured project notes into a clearer first draft, but polished language is not evidence of accuracy. A fluent summary can confuse a proposal with an approval, remove an important qualification or invent a reason for a variance.

Start with a narrow task, approved information, explicit boundaries and a named reviewer. The workflow below is an original reporting example intended to help a team design controls. It does not endorse a product or promise a productivity saving.

## Choose a task you can check

Begin with an internal narrative draft from verified records. Avoid starting with autonomous changes to budgets, schedules, purchase orders or external communications. Limit the tool's role to assistance with language and structure.

The UK Government's [AI Playbook](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government/artificial-intelligence-playbook-for-the-uk-government-html) emphasises understanding limitations, suitable uses, security and meaningful human control. This workflow applies those general principles to a fictional reporting exercise; it is not a government-mandated process.

## Step 1: Agree the information boundary

Confirm the organisation permits the tool and proposed data use. Check who can access its workspace and the rules for input retention and reuse. Use only information authorised for that purpose.

Use fictional records for a learning exercise. For a real report, the appropriate internal specialists should determine what can be shared. Replacing a customer's name alone may not remove confidentiality concerns: dates, values, technical details and combinations of facts can still reveal a project.

Record who approved the information boundary and the permitted audience. Permission to draft an internal report does not automatically authorise customer distribution or online publication.

## Step 2: Prepare a small evidence pack

Give inputs a cut-off, record identifiers and clear statuses. Separate facts, assumptions, proposals and approvals before asking the tool to write.

| Record | Fictional input |
| --- | --- |
| M-14 | Design approval forecast moved from 6 May to 9 May; reason awaiting confirmation |
| A-08 | Delivery lead to confirm downstream effect before the next review |
| C-03 | Overtime proposal submitted; no approval recorded |

These records contain deliberate gaps. The draft should preserve them, not supply a plausible explanation. The inputs do not prove an overall completion delay and do not authorise overtime.

## Step 3: Give an explicit drafting brief

For the fictional pack, this is a starting point:

Draft an internal update using only the supplied records. Keep record identifiers beside factual statements. Separate confirmed information, unresolved questions and decisions required. Do not invent causes, dates, costs, approvals or completion forecasts. State what must be checked if evidence is missing. Do not perform calculations or act in other systems. Return a draft for human review.

Adapt the brief to your purpose and test the selected tool with incomplete or contradictory inputs. A prompt is an instruction, not a guarantee of correct behaviour.

## Step 4: Verify claims against the records

Compare every material statement with its source. Check numbers independently in the approved calculation or planning system. Verify names, dates, status language and implied causal relationships.

For M-14, the draft may say design approval is forecast three calendar days later. It must not claim a supplier caused the movement: the reason is unconfirmed. It must not declare overall completion three days late, because downstream effects have not been assessed. Even the working-day impact requires the relevant calendar.

For C-03, the report should say a proposal awaits a decision. Writing that overtime is approved changes the meaning and could prompt unauthorised action. Reject that wording and retain the correction for the next evaluation.

## Step 5: Approve through the normal route

A named person remains accountable for the released update. Retain the input pack, draft, corrections, final version and approval according to the organisation's information-management arrangements.

Limit permissions to the task. A narrative drafting tool does not need authority to edit the schedule or send the report. Treat any later automated distribution as a separately authorised workflow with defined controls and a way to stop it.

## Step 6: Check whether the workflow is worthwhile

Review a small set of permitted examples before expanding. Include missing data, contradictory dates, pending approvals and an event with no confirmed cause. Compare output with a manually prepared reference.

Track errors, review effort and the usefulness of the final report. A draft that is quicker to generate but harder to verify may not improve reporting. Claim a percentage saving only after measuring the complete workflow, including correction and approval.

## Your first controlled exercise

Use the three fictional records above to prepare a report manually, then compare it with an AI-assisted draft. Identify unsupported claims and lost qualifications. Agree acceptance checks before considering workplace input.

For the report structure, see our [PMO dashboard guide](/articles/pmo-dashboard-that-supports-decisions). Our [integrated baseline guide](/articles/integrated-project-baseline-practical-guide) explains why reliable input remains essential.

## Professional reading

- [UK Government: Artificial Intelligence Playbook](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/ai-playbook-for-the-uk-government/artificial-intelligence-playbook-for-the-uk-government-html)

The records, dates and brief are fictional learning material. Live use requires relevant employer permissions and organisational controls.
